original_value: With people moving out of physical public spaces due to containment measures to tackle the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, online platforms become even more prominent tools to understand social discussion. Studying social media can be informative to assess how we are collectively coping with this unprecedented global crisis. However, social media platforms are also populated by bots, automated accounts that can amplify certain topics of discussion at the expense of others. In this paper, we study 43.3M English tweets about COVID-19 and provide early evidence of the use of bots to promote political conspiracies in the United States, in stark contrast with humans who focus on public health concerns.

result.paraphrase: As containment measures for the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic pushed people out of physical public spaces, online platforms became even more important for understanding social discourse. Analyzing social media can help assess how we are collectively coping with this unprecedented global crisis. Yet these platforms also contain bots—automated accounts that can elevate some topics over others. In this paper, we examine 43.3M English tweets about COVID-19 and present early evidence that bots were used to promote political conspiracies in the United States, while humans focused on public health concerns.
